Tutorial: Subgroup Cox Forest Plots Using the lung Dataset

Example analysis

Overview

This tutorial demonstrates how to use cox_subgroup_forest() with the built-in lung dataset from the survival package.

The function was written to create publication-style subgroup forest plots from treatment-effect Cox proportional-hazards models. It fits

Surv(time, event) ~ treatment

within each subgroup and reports hazard ratios (HRs), 95% confidence intervals, p-values, sample sizes, events, and median survival by arm.

Important: lung does not contain a randomised treatment variable. For a software demonstration, this tutorial uses sex as the two-level comparison variable. The resulting HRs are observational sex comparisons, not treatment effects.

1. Packages

library(survival)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

source("forestplot_favouring_function.R")

The main function also uses broom, purrr, ggplot2, forestploter, tibble, stringr, and grid.

2. Load the lung data

data("lung", package = "survival")
## Warning in data("lung", package = "survival"): data set 'lung' not found
dim(lung)
## [1] 228  10
head(lung)
##   inst time status age sex ph.ecog ph.karno pat.karno meal.cal wt.loss
## 1    3  306      2  74   1       1       90       100     1175      NA
## 2    3  455      2  68   1       0       90        90     1225      15
## 3    3 1010      1  56   1       0       90        90       NA      15
## 4    5  210      2  57   1       1       90        60     1150      11
## 5    1  883      2  60   1       0      100        90       NA       0
## 6   12 1022      1  74   1       1       50        80      513       0

The key variables used here are:

  • time: observed survival time;
  • status: censoring/event indicator;
  • sex: coded as 1/2;
  • ph.ecog: ECOG performance status; and
  • age: patient age.

3. Prepare the analysis dataset

The requested transformation is applied below.

df <- lung %>%
  mutate(
    sex        = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    ecog       = factor(
      ph.ecog,
      levels = c(0, 1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("ECOG 0", "ECOG 1", "ECOG 2", "ECOG 3")
    ),
    age_grp    = factor(
      ifelse(age < 63, "Age < 63", "Age >= 63")
    ),
    status_bin = as.numeric(status == 2)
  ) %>%
  drop_na(time, status_bin, sex, ecog, age_grp, age)

df %>%
  count(sex)
##      sex   n
## 1   Male 137
## 2 Female  90
df %>%
  count(ecog)
##     ecog   n
## 1 ECOG 0  63
## 2 ECOG 1 113
## 3 ECOG 2  50
## 4 ECOG 3   1
df %>%
  count(age_grp)
##     age_grp   n
## 1  Age < 63 105
## 2 Age >= 63 122

status_bin is coded as 1 for the event and 0 for censoring.

4. Define the comparison arms

The function requires exactly two treatment levels. Because lung has no treatment variable, the demonstration uses sex:

table(df$sex)
## 
##   Male Female 
##    137     90
arm_order <- c("Male", "Female")
arm_labels <- c("Male", "Female")

This means the fitted model coefficient represents:

Male vs Female

and HR < 1 corresponds to lower hazard in males relative to females.

Again, this is only a demonstration of the function.

5. Run the subgroup forest analysis

We will examine two subgroup variables:

  • ECOG performance status;
  • age group.
result <- cox_subgroup_forest(
  data = df,
  covariates = c("ecog", "age_grp"),
  labels = c(
    "ECOG performance status",
    "Age group"
  ),
  treatment = "sex",
  time = "time",
  event = "status_bin",
  endpoint_labels = "Overall survival",
  arm_order = arm_order,
  treatment_labels = arm_labels,
  palette = "grey30",
  time_unit = "months",
  length_plot = 60,
  ci_pch = 15, 
  ci_lty = 1,
  ci_lwd = 3, 
  ci_Theight = 0.4, 
  sizes = 1
)

6. Examine the results table

result$results_table
## # A tibble: 8 × 14
##   covariate covariate_label        subgroup indent endpoint endpoint_label     n
##   <chr>     <chr>                  <chr>    <lgl>  <chr>    <chr>          <int>
## 1 ecog      ECOG performance stat… All pat… FALSE  time     Overall survi…   227
## 2 ecog      ECOG performance stat… ECOG 0   TRUE   time     Overall survi…    63
## 3 ecog      ECOG performance stat… ECOG 1   TRUE   time     Overall survi…   113
## 4 ecog      ECOG performance stat… ECOG 2   TRUE   time     Overall survi…    50
## 5 ecog      ECOG performance stat… ECOG 3   TRUE   time     Overall survi…     1
## 6 age_grp   Age group              All pat… FALSE  time     Overall survi…   227
## 7 age_grp   Age group              Age < 63 TRUE   time     Overall survi…   105
## 8 age_grp   Age group              Age >= … TRUE   time     Overall survi…   122
## # ℹ 7 more variables: n_event <dbl>, median_a <dbl>, median_b <dbl>, hr <dbl>,
## #   conf_low <dbl>, conf_high <dbl>, p_value <dbl>

The table contains:

  • subgroup: subgroup definition;
  • n: number of observations used;
  • n_event: number of events;
  • median_a: median survival for Arm A;
  • median_b: median survival for Arm B;
  • hr: hazard ratio;
  • conf_low and conf_high: 95% CI;
  • p_value: Wald p-value from the Cox model.

For this example, Arm A is Male and Arm B is Female.

7. Median survival table

A compact median-survival table is available:

result$median_survival_table
## # A tibble: 8 × 7
##   covariate_label         subgroup     endpoint_label      n n_event median_Male
##   <chr>                   <chr>        <chr>           <int>   <dbl>       <dbl>
## 1 ECOG performance status All patients Overall surviv…   227     164         270
## 2 ECOG performance status ECOG 0       Overall surviv…    63      37         353
## 3 ECOG performance status ECOG 1       Overall surviv…   113      82         239
## 4 ECOG performance status ECOG 2       Overall surviv…    50      44         166
## 5 ECOG performance status ECOG 3       Overall surviv…     1       1         118
## 6 Age group               All patients Overall surviv…   227     164         270
## 7 Age group               Age < 63     Overall surviv…   105      72         286
## 8 Age group               Age >= 63    Overall surviv…   122      92         270
## # ℹ 1 more variable: median_Female <dbl>

This can be useful when creating supplementary tables or checking the values displayed in the forest plot.

8. Plot ECOG subgroup results

The function returns a forest plot for each covariate.

result$plots[["ECOG performance status"]]

The plot contains an All patients estimate followed by the individual ECOG subgroups.

The x-axis is logarithmic and the vertical reference line is HR = 1.

9. Plot age-group results

result$plots[["Age group"]]

The same modelling and display approach is used for the age subgroups.

10. Combined forest plot

A combined forest plot is also returned:

result$combined_plots

This provides a compact overview of the subgroup estimates from both covariates.

11. Access the fitted Cox models

The fitted models are stored in result$models.

names(result$models)
## [1] "ECOG performance status" "Age group"
names(result$models[["ECOG performance status"]])
## [1] "ECOG performance status | All patients | Overall survival"
## [2] "ECOG performance status | ECOG 0 | Overall survival"      
## [3] "ECOG performance status | ECOG 1 | Overall survival"      
## [4] "ECOG performance status | ECOG 2 | Overall survival"

A particular model can be extracted and inspected with standard survival methods:

fit <- result$models[["ECOG performance status"]][[
  "ECOG performance status | ECOG 2 | Overall survival"
]]

summary(fit)
## Call:
## survival::coxph(formula = fmla, data = d)
## 
##   n= 50, number of events= 44 
## 
##           coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z Pr(>|z|)
## sexMale 0.3638    1.4387   0.3189 1.141    0.254
## 
##         exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
## sexMale     1.439      0.695    0.7701     2.688
## 
## Concordance= 0.581  (se = 0.04 )
## Likelihood ratio test= 1.33  on 1 df,   p=0.2
## Wald test            = 1.3  on 1 df,   p=0.3
## Score (logrank) test = 1.32  on 1 df,   p=0.3

The exact subgroup names available depend on the data after missing-value filtering.

12. Continuous covariates

The function can also treat a numeric covariate as continuous.

For example, use age directly:

result_age <- cox_subgroup_forest(
  data = df,
  covariates = c("age"),
  labels = c("Age"),
  treatment = "sex",
  time = "time",
  event = "status_bin",
  endpoint_labels = "Overall survival",
  continuous_vars = "age",
  arm_order = arm_order,
  treatment_labels = arm_labels,
  palette = "grey30",
  time_unit = "months"
)

For the forest plot, age is divided at its median into two groups. The function also returns a separate per-unit effect:

result_age$continuous_effects
## # A tibble: 1 × 10
##   covariate covariate_label endpoint endpoint_label      hr conf_low conf_high
##   <chr>     <chr>           <chr>    <chr>            <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
## 1 age       Age             time     Overall survival  1.02    0.998      1.04
## # ℹ 3 more variables: p_value <dbl>, n <int>, interpretation <chr>

This is an important distinction:

  • the forest-plot rows estimate the Male vs Female hazard ratio within age-defined groups;
  • continuous_effects estimates the hazard ratio associated with a one-unit increase in age, adjusted for treatment through stratification.

These are different quantities.

13. Interpreting an HR

If a row has an HR such as:

0.70 (0.50-0.98)

the estimate is a 30% lower hazard for Arm A relative to Arm B, with a 95% CI from 0.50 to 0.98.

The direction follows the function’s fixed coding:

HR = Arm A / Arm B

In this tutorial:

Arm A = Male
Arm B = Female

Therefore, the interpretation is a comparison of males with females.

14. Changing the length of the plot and the ticks and x limits

Automatically, there will be 5 ticks and labels and the length is 40 spaces.

result <- cox_subgroup_forest(
  data = df,
  covariates = c("ecog", "age_grp"),
  labels = c(
    "ECOG performance status",
    "Age group"
  ),
  treatment = "sex",
  time = "time",
  event = "status_bin",
  endpoint_labels = "Overall survival",
  arm_order = arm_order,
  treatment_labels = arm_labels,
  palette = "grey30",
  time_unit = "months",
  length_plot = 50,
  xlim = c(0.5, 6),
  ticks_at = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4),
  ci_pch = 20, 
  ci_lty = 1,
  ci_lwd = 3, 
  ci_Theight = 0.4, 
  sizes = 1
)
result$combined_plots

15. Exporting results

The results table is an ordinary data frame, so it can be exported with standard R tools:

write.csv(
  result$results_table,
  "lung_subgroup_cox_results.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

The forest plot object can be drawn on a graphics device such as PDF or PNG using standard R graphics workflows. The supplied function itself returns forestploter objects rather than writing files automatically.

16. Recommended use with real trial data

For a real randomised trial, replace the demonstration sex variable with the actual two-level treatment-arm variable.

For example:

result <- cox_subgroup_forest(
  data = trial_data,
  covariates = c("sex", "age_grp", "ecog"),
  labels = c("Sex", "Age group", "ECOG"),
  treatment = "treatment",
  time = "os_time",
  event = "os_event",
  endpoint_labels = "Overall survival",
  arm_order = c("Treatment A", "Treatment B"),
  treatment_labels = c("Treatment A", "Treatment B"),
  palette = "grey30"
)

For formal subgroup inference, do not rely on within-subgroup p-values alone. A treatment-by-subgroup interaction analysis is generally needed to test whether treatment effects differ between subgroups.

17. Summary

The key workflow is:

  1. load the survival data;
  2. create appropriately coded variables;
  3. identify a two-level treatment variable;
  4. specify subgroup covariates;
  5. pair survival time and event variables;
  6. run cox_subgroup_forest();
  7. inspect results_table;
  8. inspect the individual or combined forest plots; and
  9. interpret the HR according to the specified arm_order.

The lung example is intended to make the code reproducible and easy to learn. It should not be interpreted as a causal treatment analysis.
